messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Since the accident, Rajesh Patel, a 58-year-old fisherman, has organized his life around a sense that danger can break in without warning. He had spent most of his adult life working on the water along the Gulf Coast, leaving before dawn, reading weather by habit, and trusting the routines of his body and boat. The accident happened on a gray morning when he was driving to the marina before sunrise. The roads were nearly empty, and the quiet had felt ordinary at first, the kind of heavy predawn silence he had known for years. Then another car came into his lane and struck his truck hard enough that the world became metal, glass, and the violent force of impact. He remembers the image of the other vehicle at the moment of collision with a vividness that still jolts him. In his recollection there is the sudden sight of headlights and crumpled steel, then the bodily certainty that he might die there before anyone reached him.

What has troubled him afterward is not only that he remembers it, but that the memory does not feel like a memory. When it comes, it arrives as if the crash is happening again in the present. He has told the therapist, haltingly, that he knows what happened, but when he tries to put it into words he gets stuck. He can start with the drive to work or the empty road, but then language seems to fall away and what takes over instead is the same terror he felt inside the wrecked truck. At those moments his body reacts before he can steady himself, and he is left feeling ashamed and unsettled by how little control he seems to have. He has come to believe that his body is no longer reliable, that the instincts and physical steadiness he depended on for a lifetime at sea cannot be counted on anymore.

Over the months that followed, ordinary parts of daily life became difficult in ways that felt humiliating to him. At the marina, where fishermen and dockworkers are always crossing paths with buyers, mechanics, and tourists, even casual conversation with someone he does not know can put him on edge. A stranger asking a simple question about the catch or the weather can make him feel braced, watchful, unsure of what the person really wants. He has grown convinced that people are not what they seem, and this wariness has narrowed his world. He keeps interactions short, avoids eye contact when he can, and lets others handle conversations that used to come easily enough. The changes have not been lost on the people around him. Men who once knew him as steady and sociable now find him withdrawn and curt, and Rajesh feels that some essential version of himself has gone missing. He says he no longer knows himself.

Certain reminders cut straight through whatever composure he is trying to maintain. If he sees images of cars mangled in an accident, whether on the roadside or on television, he feels the moment collapse into the present. News or casual talk about someone losing a loved one is also hard for him to bear. Since being widowed, those conversations land with particular force, and he finds himself pulling away before anyone notices the shift in his face. He does not explain much. Partly this is because he cannot find the words, and partly because he does not trust where the conversation will go once it begins.

Silence has become its own warning sign. On the water, he once relied on quiet as part of the job, but now unusual silence makes him feel that something dangerous is about to happen. If the house goes still at night, he does not experience that stillness as peace. He listens into it, alert, scanning for what might be wrong. Even inside his own home, he rarely feels off duty. He checks sounds, looks out windows, notices movements outside, and tracks small changes in the environment as if vigilance might keep another catastrophe from striking. This same scanning follows him to the docks, to parking lots, to the drive to work. He studies other cars, other drivers, other people’s faces.

What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was not one dramatic moment but the accumulation of these changes. He was tired of living as if danger were always one silent second away. He was troubled by how small his life had become, how often he avoided people, and how easily his mind was captured by the image of collision. Most of all, he was frightened by the feeling that neither other people nor his own body could be trusted, and that the man who had spent decades making his living in difficult conditions had been replaced by someone perpetually on guard. He came to treatment hoping, cautiously, that he might find a way to speak about what happened without being thrown back into it, and fearing that if he could not, this tense and unfamiliar version of his life would be permanent.
